'''''Solanum dulcamara''''' is a [[species]] of [[vine]] in the genus ''[[Solanum]]'' (which also includes the [[potato]] and the [[tomato]]) of the family [[Solanaceae]]. Common names include  '''bittersweet''', '''bittersweet nightshade''', '''bitter nightshade''', '''blue bindweed''', '''Amara Dulcis''',<ref>[http://medherb.com/culpeper_names.html Culpeper Plant Names Database], discussing various editions of [[Nicholas Culpeper|Culpeper]], for example Culpeper, Nicholas, ''The English physitian: or an astrologo-physical discourse of the vulgar herbs of this nation'', London, Peter Cole, 1652.</ref> '''climbing nightshade''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SODU|taxon=Solanum dulcamara|access-date=17 November 2015}}</ref> '''felonwort''', '''fellenwort''', '''felonwood''', '''poisonberry''', '''poisonflower''', '''scarlet berry''', '''[[Snake berry|snakeberry]]''',<ref name="blanchan">{{cite book |author=Blanchan, Neltje |title=Wild Flowers Worth Knowing |year=2005 |publisher=[[Project Gutenberg|Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation]] |author-link=Neltje Blanchan|title-link=Wild Flowers Worth Knowing }}</ref><ref>"Almost any unfamiliar berry is or may be snake-berry, and all snake-berries are poisonous; so a boy dares not eat a berry till some one...".  Needs verification but may come from {{cite journal |title=Popular American Plant Names |author=Fannie D. Bergen |journal=Botanical Gazette |issue=11 |date=November 1892 |pages=363–380 |volume=17 |doi=10.1086/326860 |s2cid=224830265 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/partpdf/222200 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Guide to Poisonous and Toxic Plants (Technical Guide #196) |date=July 1994 |url=http://chppm-www.apgea.army.mil/ento/WILD_P-Z.HTM#SDULCAMARA |publisher=US Army center for health promotion and preventive medicine, Entomological Sciences Program |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080504134725/http://chppm-www.apgea.army.mil/ento/WILD_P-Z.HTM |archive-date=May 4, 2008 }}</ref> '''trailing bittersweet''', '''trailing nightshade''', '''violet bloom''', and '''woody nightshade'''.

It is native to Europe and Asia, and widely naturalised elsewhere, including [[North America]].

==Overview==
[[File:Solanum-dulcamara-Distribution-PhytoKeys-022-001-g036.jpg|thumb|left|Distribution of ''S. dulcamara''.]]

It occurs in a very wide range of [[Habitat (ecology)|habitats]], from [[woodland]]s to [[scrubland]], [[hedge (gardening)|hedge]]s and [[marsh]]es.

''Solanum dulcamara'' is a semi-woody [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[vine]], which scrambles over other plants, capable of reaching a height of 4 m where suitable support is available, but more often 1–2 m high. The leaves are 4–12 cm long, roughly arrowhead-shaped, and often lobed at the base. The flowers are in loose clusters of 3–20, 1–1.5 cm across, star-shaped, with five purple petals and yellow stamens and style pointing forward. The fruit is an ovoid red [[berry (botany)|berry]] about 1 cm long,<ref>{{cite book | last1=Parnell | first1=John A. N. | last2=Cullen | first2=Elaine L. | last3=Webb | first3=D. A. | last4=Curtis | first4=Tom | title=Webb's an Irish flora | publisher=Cork University Press | publication-place=Cork | date=2011 | isbn=978-1-909005-08-2 | oclc=830022856}}</ref> soft and juicy, with the aspect and odour of a tiny tomato, and edible for some birds, which disperse the seeds widely.{{Citation needed|date=July 2011}} However, the berry is poisonous to humans and livestock,<ref name="Chesnut1898">{{cite book |author=Victor King Chesnut | author-link=Victor King Chesnut |title=Thirty Poisonous Plants of the United States |url=https://archive.org/details/CAT87202204 |access-date=2017-07-22 |year=1898 |publisher=U.S. Department of Agriculture |pages=31–32 |chapter=Bittersweet |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/CAT87202204/page/n31}}</ref><ref name="Quattrocchi2016">{{cite book |author=Umberto Quattrocchi| title=CRC World Dictionary of Medicinal and Poisonous Plants: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymology (5 Volume Set) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-37OBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA3489 |access-date=2017-07-22 |year=2016 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4822-5064-0 |page=3481}}</ref> and the berry's attractive and familiar look makes it dangerous for children.

It has a long flowering season and can flower from May through November.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.html?sub=6448|title=bittersweet nightshade: Solanum dulcamara (Solanales: Solanaceae): Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States|website=Invasiveplantatlas.org|access-date=July 31, 2026}}</ref>Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 19.5 days, and bears an average of 17.9 seeds per fruit. Fruits average 84.1% water.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}}

It is native to northern Africa, Europe, and Asia, but has spread throughout the world. The plant is relatively important in the diet of some species of birds such as European [[Thrush (bird)|thrushes]],<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jones |first1=Theresa |title=Climbing nightshade |url=https://www.gcc.mass.edu/oll/plants/climbing-nightshade/ |website=Outdoor Learning Lab |publisher=Greenfield Community College |access-date=4 April 2021}}</ref> which feed on its fruits, being immune to its poisons, and scatter the seeds abroad. It grows in all types of terrain with a preference for wetlands<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Solanum dulcamara |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/shrub/soldul/all.html |access-date=2022-10-10 |publisher=US Forest Service}}</ref> and the [[understory]] of [[riparian forests]]. Along with other climbers, it creates a dark and impenetrable shelter for varied animals. The plant grows well in dark areas in places where it can receive the light of morning or afternoon. An area receiving bright light for many hours reduces its development.<ref name=":0" /> It grows more easily in rich wet soils with plenty of nitrogen. When grown for medicinal purposes, it is best grown in a dry, exposed environment.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Solanum dulcamara Bittersweet. Bittersweet Nightshade, Climbing nightshade, Bittersweet, Deadly Nightshade, Poisonous PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Solanum+dulcamara |access-date=2022-10-10 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref>

It is a nonnative species in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |title=Solanum dulcamara |publisher=US Forest Service |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/shrub/soldul/all.html |access-date=2022-08-25}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Illustration Solanum dulcamara0.jpg|thumb|Illustration by Kurt Stüber, published in Prof. Dr. Otto Wilhelm Thomé, ''Flora von Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz'', 1885, Gera, Germany.]]

''Solanum dulcamara'' has been valued by [[herbalists]] since ancient Greek times. In the Middle Ages the plant was thought to be effective against witchcraft, and was sometimes hung around the neck of cattle to protect them from the "[[evil eye]]".<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=d25jAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA39|page=39|title=Daimonomageia. A small treatise of sicknesses and diseases from witchcraft and supernatural causes, etc.|author=Drage, William|year=1665}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x0ks6JPrsngC&pg=PP12|pages=1–2|title=Culpeper's Complete Herbal & English Physician|author=Culpeper, Nicholas|author-link=Nicholas Culpeper|isbn=9781557090805|date=October 2006 |publisher=Applewood Books}}</ref><ref name="grieve" /> It has been suggested that the plant was used both medicinally and to induce altered states of mind in [[Anglo-Saxon England]].<ref name="alarichall">Alaric Hall, "[http://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/78177 Madness, Medication—and Self-Induced Hallucination? ''Elleborus'' (and Woody Nightshade) in Anglo-Saxon England, 700–900]", ''Leeds Studies in English'', new series, [https://archive.org/details/lse-2013-whole-issue 44] (2013), 43-69 (pp. 60–62).</ref> The monk and scholar [[Aldhelm]] of Malmesbury (c. 639-709) included a riddle about this plant in his [[Epistola ad Acircium]], describing its effects as inflicting a "touch of insanity" upon the user, leaving them "mad with dizziness."<ref name="alarichall"></ref> An eleventh-century herbarium also records the name "madness-berry" for this plant (''wedeberge'').<ref>Vriend, Hubert Jan de (ed.). 1984. The Old English Herbarium and Medicina de Quadrupedibus, The Early English Text Society, 286 (London: Oxford University Press)</ref>

[[John Gerard]]'s ''Herball'' (1597) states that "the juice is good for those that have fallen from high places, and have been thereby bruised or beaten, for it is thought to dissolve blood congealed or cluttered anywhere in the intrals and to heale the hurt places."<ref name="grieve">{{cite book|title=A Modern Herbal: The Medicinal, Culinary, Cosmetic and Economic Properties, Cultivation and Folk-lore of Herbs, Grasses, Fungi, Shrubs, & Trees with All Their Modern Scientific Uses, Volume 1|author=Grieve, Maud|year=1971}}</ref>

==Biological activity==
This plant is one of the less poisonous members of the Solanaceae. Instances of poisoning in humans are very rare on account of the fruit's intensely bitter taste. Incidentally, the fruit has been reported to have a sweet aftertaste, hence the vernacular name ''bittersweet''.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Mabey | first1=Richard | last2=Gibbons | first2=Bob | last3=Jones | first3=Gareth Lovett | title=Flora Britannica | publisher=Chatto & Windus | publication-place=London | date=1997 | isbn=1-85619-377-2 | oclc=38725904}}</ref>

The poison in this species is believed to be solanine.<ref>{{cite journal |title=A Fatal Case of Solanine Poisoning |author1=R. F. Alexander |author2=G. B. Forbes |author3=E. S. Hawkins  |name-list-style=amp |journal=Br Med J |date=1948-09-11 |volume=2 |issue=4575 |page=518 |pmc=2091497 |doi=10.1136/bmj.2.4575.518 |pmid=18881287}}</ref> The alkaloids, [[solanine]] (from unripe fruits), [[solasodine]] (from flowers) and beta-solamarine (from roots) have been found to inhibit the growth of ''[[E. coli]]'' and ''[[Staphylococcus aureus|S. aureus]]''.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Kumar | first1=Padma | last2=Sharma | first2=Bindu | last3=Bakshi | first3=Nidhi | title=Biological activity of alkaloids from ''Solanum dulcamara'' L. | journal=Natural Product Research | publisher=Informa UK Limited | volume=23 | issue=8 | date=2009-05-20 | issn=1478-6419 | doi=10.1080/14786410802267692 | pages=719–723| pmid=19418354 | s2cid=25721657 }}</ref> Solanine and solasodine  extracted from ''Solanum dulcamara'' showed antidermatophytic activity against ''Chrysosporium indicum'', ''[[Trichophyton mentagrophytes]]'' and ''T. simil'', thus it may cure [[ringworm]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bakshi |first1=N. |last2=Kumar |first2=P. |last3=Sharma |first3=M. |title=Antidermatophytic activity of some alkaloids from ''Solanum dulcamara'' |journal=Indian Drugs |volume=45 |issue=6 |pages=483–484 |year=2008}}</ref>

The stems are approved by the [[German Commission E]] for external use as supportive therapy in chronic [[eczema]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/bittersweet-nightshade.html |title=Bittersweet Nightshade |publisher=Drugs.com |access-date=2013-08-15}}</ref>

== Medicinal use ==
''Solanum dulcamara'' has a variety of documented medicinal uses, all of which are advised to be approached with proper caution as the entirety of the plant is considered to be poisonous. Always seek advice from a professional before using a plant medicinally. There have only been records of medicinal use for adults (not children) and it is possible to be allergic to ''Solanum dulcamara;'' medicinal use is not advised in these cases.<ref name=":03">{{Cite web |date=15 January 2013 |title=Community herbal monograph on Solanum dulcamara L., stipites |url=https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/herbal-monograph/final-community-herbal-monograph-solanum-dulcamara-l-stipites_en.pdf |website=European Medicines Agency Science Medicines Health}}</ref>

=== Use of stem ===
The stem of ''Solanum dulcamara'' is believed to be considerably less poisonous than the rest of the plant, and it has mostly been used in treatment for conditions of the skin. There are records of it being used to treat mild recurrent [[eczema]], [[psoriasis]], [[scabies]], and [[dermatomycosis]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=12 July 2013 |title=Woody nightshade stem |url=https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/herbal-summary/woody-nightshade-stem-summary-public_en.pdf |website=European Medicines Agency Science Medicines Health}}</ref><ref name=":32">{{Cite web |title=Целебные Травы {{!}} Паслен сладко-горький - Solanum dulcamara L. |url=http://www.medherb.ru/sol_du.htm |access-date=2022-10-10 |website=Medherb.ru}}</ref> Stems are harvested when they do not yet have leaves (or the leaves have already fallen) and are shredded into small pieces. They are mostly known to be applied in the form of liquid onto the skin, but infusing it into a drink is also possible, though not recommended.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=Solanum dulcamara Bittersweet. Bittersweet Nightshade, Climbing nightshade, Bittersweet, Deadly Nightshade, Poisonous PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Solanum+dulcamara |access-date=2022-10-03 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref> The stem has also been used in treatment for [[bronchitis]], [[asthma]], and [[pneumonia]].<ref name=":32" />

=== Use of leaves, fruit, and root ===
The leaves of ''Solanum dulcamara'' have been known to treat [[Wart|warts]] and [[tumors]], while the fruit can treat conditions of the respiratory tract and joints.<ref name=":03" /> It has been documented that Indigenous people of North America used the roots for relief of [[fever]] and [[nausea]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=BRIT - Native American Ethnobotany Database |url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/species/3719/ |access-date=2022-10-05 |website=naeb.brit.org}}</ref>

== Symbolism ==
''Solanum dulcamara'' has been used as a symbol of [[fidelity]]. This is in reference to its curious property of combining extreme bitterness with surprising sweetness – hence its common name "bittersweet". This symbolism is seen in Christian art from the Middle Ages as well as in bridal wreaths.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kandeler |first1=Riklef |last2=Ullrich |first2=Wolfram R. |date=2009 |title=Symbolism of plants: examples from European-Mediterranean culture presented with biology and history of art |journal=Journal of Experimental Botany |volume=60 |issue=11 |pages=2955–2956 |doi=10.1093/jxb/erp207 |jstor=24038282 |pmid=19549625 |issn=0022-0957|doi-access=free }}</ref>
